newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African CPI at year high, but better than feared.
newsitem.headline: S.African CPI at year high, but better than feared.

text.p: South African consumer price inflation rose to 7.5 percent year-on-year, its highest level since August last year when it also stood at 7.5 percent.
But the data, released at 0900 GMT, was slightly better than expected. The consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters was for a 7.7 percent annual increase, up from July's 7.1 percent.

The Central Statistical Service said the increase in the inflation rate for the fourth consecutive month was driven primarily by food price rises which accounted for 0.4 point of a percentage point to the 0.5 month-on-month increase in the CPI.
Housing costs accounted for 0.1 point and all other items 0.1 point.
These increases were slightly offset by a 0.1 point decrease in transport, reflecting last month's six cent a litre decrease in gasoline prices.
The monthly increase in the CPI excluding food was 0.2 percent.

Year-on-year, the food price index leapt to 7.9 percent in August from 4.8 percent in July, driven by higher month-on-month costs across the board, with the exception of fish. Vegetables registered the greatest increase which increased in price by 6.4 percent from July to August.
"It's the first time in a long while that food inflation has been higher than non-food inflation...It's a good performance on the non-food side," said Nick Barnardt, BOE NatWest strategic economist.
Bonds showed little reaction to the data with the benchmark R150 standing at a yield of 14.935 percent from 14.945 before the release and 14.975 on Wednesday.
Barnardt said he still expected the CPI rate to reach around 8.5 percent by the year-end with food likely to accelerate to 10 percent.

For September, the CSS said that in addition to the normal price surveys, changed prices would also apply to certain urban areas' water tariffs, electricity, assessment rates, refuse removal and sanitary services.
